q: What are the different types of waves?
What is the difference between wind waves and swell?
What are the parts of a wave?
How do waves travel across the ocean?
a: Ocean waves are primarily formed by wind blowing across the water surface, transferring energy from the atmosphere to the ocean. Wind waves are generated locally by the wind and have steep, chaotic shapes, while swell consists of longer-wavelength, more organized waves that have traveled beyond their generation area and can cross entire ocean basins. Wave properties include wavelength (distance between successive crests), wave height (vertical distance from trough to crest), period (time between successive crests), and frequency. Tsunamis are a distinct type of wave generated by seafloor displacement during earthquakes, landslides, or volcanic eruptions, with very long wavelengths (up to 200 km) and speeds exceeding 700 km/h in deep water.

q: What are spring and neap tides?
How do the Moon and Sun affect tides?
Why are there two high tides per day?
a: Tides are the rhythmic rise and fall of sea level caused primarily by the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun on Earth's oceans, combined with Earth's rotation. Spring tides occur during new and full moons when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are aligned, producing the greatest tidal range (highest high tides and lowest low tides). Neap tides occur during first and third quarter moons when the Sun and Moon pull at right angles, producing the smallest tidal range. Most coastal areas experience two high tides and two low tides per day (semidiurnal tides) because the tidal bulges on both the near and far sides of Earth pass a given location as Earth rotates.

q: What equipment is used to measure tides?
a: Tide prediction is based on harmonic analysis, which decomposes the complex tidal signal into hundreds of individual tidal constituents, each corresponding to a specific gravitational effect of the Moon, Sun, and planetary motions. Tide gauges and satellite altimeters measure water levels continuously, providing data used to generate tide tables and predictions years in advance, accurate to within a few centimeters. Local factors such as coastal geography, water depth, wind, and atmospheric pressure can significantly modify predicted tides, producing storm surges and other non-tidal water level variations.

q: How is wave energy converted into electricity?
What are the advantages of wave power?
What are the challenges of wave energy?
How much energy can waves produce?
a: Wave energy is the capture of ocean wave motion to generate electricity, representing a largely untapped renewable energy source with high power density compared to wind or solar. Wave energy converters (WECs) use various technologies — including oscillating water columns (that drive air turbines), point absorbers (buoy-like devices), and attenuators (long articulated structures aligned with wave direction, like the Pelamis) — to convert the mechanical energy of waves into electrical power. While wave energy is more predictable and consistent than solar or wind and has minimal visual impact when installed offshore, challenges include high installation and maintenance costs, marine corrosion, survivability in storms, and environmental impacts on marine ecosystems.
